construction_notes: Replacement rate = net income from pensions and transfers at age 68 (2018) divided by average income at ages 57–59 (2007–09).
Numerator: (i) private pensions = occupational (pillar 2) plus private (pillar 3); (ii) public pensions = the PAYG means-tested component (pillar 1); (iii) other public transfers to the elderly.

Denominator: average disposable income at 57–59 = total earnings including wages, public transfers and the imputed rental value of owner-occupied housing, minus taxes, interest expenses, alimony payments and similar deductions.
An average over the years just prior to retirement is used to avoid jumps in income ahead of retirement from part-time and retirement anticipation schemes.
Wealth is gross wealth: all liquid (financial assets and bank liquidity) and illiquid (house, vehicles and other equities) assets.
Housing wealth starts from DPAA assessments and is adjusted by Statistics Denmark using market values imputed from sales statistics and the register of buildings and dwellings.
Net home equity = gross home equity minus the debt secured against the house; the authors use a conservative perimeter that includes all loans secured against the house, not only mortgage debt.

Annuitisation: equation (1), with the interest rate R set to zero in the baseline and the payout horizon set to 20 years (average remaining lifetime at 65 of 18.9 years from the Statistics Denmark five-year mortality table HISB9, rounded up).
Sensitivity calibrations: R = 4.8 per cent; horizon 25 years; horizon 15 years; risk premium of +0.2 percentage points per decile step down; home equity reduced by 18 per cent.
Figures 1 and 2 are 2018 cross-sections of the whole Danish household population and of 65-year-olds respectively, per household, and are not restricted to the 42,810-individual sample.
Page numbers throughout are PDF page indices (1–15); the printed journal pages are 195–209, i.e. PDF page + 194.
Table 1 (PDF p.11) is the paper's only numeric exhibit; Figures 1–9 are charts with no printed data labels, so every figure-based claim carries a null point estimate.
The digest supplied with this pack lists no regressions and no figures, so no exhibit ids exist: every regression_id, figure_id and source_table_id is null and locations are given in prose.

heterogeneity.dimension: pre-retirement wealth decile vs pre-retirement income decile
heterogeneity.finding: Table 1 summarises this pattern by comparing the increase in replacement rates due to home equity across income and wealth deciles. The effect of home equity on replacement rates rises monotonically with wealth, while along the income distribution it declines up to the third decile and increases thereafter.
Moreover, the growth observed across wealth deciles is substantially larger than the variation across income deciles.

As a result, when we examine income and wealth distributions separately, the retirees who beneﬁt most from releasing home equity are those at the bottom and top of the income distribution and those at the top of the wealth distribution.
